---
title: "How it works"
subtitle: "The design decisions behind DeskPets, and what broke along the way"
---

This page is the engineering view. For what the animations mean, see [Pets and states](/guide/pets-and-states.qmd). For how the artwork was made, see [Art pipeline](art-pipeline.qmd).

## Design decisions

**Telemetry-driven behavior.** The pets read CPU, RAM, swap, GPU, battery, and idle time. A calm machine gets a calm cat. Sustained high CPU gets a jumping cat. A hot GPU gets a grumpy one.

**A state machine, not an if-statement.** Ten animation states are chosen by a priority ladder with hysteresis and minimum dwell times. A CPU reading bouncing between 78% and 82% produces *one* transition, not four, so the cats don't flicker. The ladder and the thresholds are laid out in [Which one wins](/guide/pets-and-states.qmd#which-one-wins) and [No flickering](/guide/pets-and-states.qmd#no-flickering).

**Privacy by design.** The app detects whether I'm at the keyboard with `GetLastInputInfo` only. There is no keyboard hook and no record of what I type.

**Built to run next to heavy workloads.** That was the original point. Telemetry runs on its own worker thread and shuts down cleanly in about 15 ms. Sprites are decoded with Qt alone, and Pillow is deliberately not a runtime dependency.

**Built for changing art.** The sprites change independently of the code, so nothing in the code hard-codes the art. Frame rectangles, counts, durations, and loop flags all come from an atlas JSON file, and the loader never computes positions from a grid. A state whose animation isn't in the atlas yet is simply unreachable, so a new behavior can ship before its art does.

## What broke along the way

My first prototype was a sketch. I kept a [phase log](https://github.com/Suyash-Naik/DeskPets/blob/main/docs/PHASE1-LOG.md) as I went, and it records what didn't survive contact with the real machine:

- **A use-after-free in the sprite loader.** The prototype wrapped a temporary bytes object in a `QImage`. I moved to `QImage(path)` plus `copy(rect)` and dropped Pillow from the runtime.
- **An unreachable idle state.** The spec said "idle if CPU < 20% *and* RAM < 60%." I measured my own desktop, and it idles at about 70% RAM, so the idle animation could never trigger. I made idle the unconditional default and demoted RAM to a hint on the card.
- **A hang on quit.** The telemetry thread was a `while True` with no stop flag. I replaced it with a worker driven by a timer.
- **A click-through that couldn't work.** Qt's mouse-transparency flag doesn't work across processes. Only the Windows `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` style makes the OS skip the window.

I also recorded what I *didn't* solve, such as pixel art that stretches at 1.5× display scaling. The gaps are documented, not hidden.

## The Pomodoro timer {#pomodoro-timer}

The [Pomodoro timer](/guide/pomodoro.qmd) went from idea to working feature in six commits, tests included. That was possible because the UI, the telemetry, and the config were already separate. The timer is one small class, `PomodoroTimer` in `src/core/pomodoro.py`. It is a single countdown that knows nothing about the pets or the card.

- **A fixed deadline, not a tick count.** Starting it records `now + 45 minutes` on a monotonic clock, and the time remaining is always the deadline minus the current time. A once-a-second ticker only refreshes the display and notices that the deadline has passed, so a stalled app can't make the timer drift.
- **Three signals carry everything outward:** `state_changed(bool)` when it starts, is cancelled, or finishes; `ticked(int)` every second with the seconds left; and `finished()`, which fires exactly once per run and never on cancel. That is what keeps a cancelled block from triggering a celebration.
- **Small rules:** `toggle()` starts or cancels, starting during a run restarts it, and it lives on the GUI thread only. The clock can be swapped for a fake one, so tests don't wait 45 minutes.

When `finished()` fires, the app plays the chime and forces the *pleased* state for five minutes. Both lengths are in `src/config.py`.

## Building the app {#building-the-app}

DeskPets is developed as Python source, but most people shouldn't need Python to run it. The installer freezes the app into a folder of native code and wraps that folder in a Windows installer. This is what I learned doing it, including the parts that went wrong.

### Why Nuitka

I chose [Nuitka](https://nuitka.net) over PyInstaller mainly because I wanted to learn it, and because it compiles Python to C instead of bundling a bytecode interpreter. It supports Python 3.14, which is what DeskPets uses. The cost is a C compiler: Nuitka needs Visual Studio's build tools. Its fallbacks (MinGW, Zig) didn't work for Python 3.14 on my machine, so installing the "Desktop development with C++" workload was the fix.

One warning from the Nuitka PyQt6 plugin worried me: *Qt threading does not work*. DeskPets samples system metrics on a worker `QThread`, so I ran the frozen build with telemetry live before trusting it. It sampled normally, including the NVIDIA reading. That is encouraging but not a long-running soak test.

### Finding the assets when frozen

The sprite atlas used to be found relative to the source file. A frozen app has no source tree, so a build that works on my machine could fail on yours. `config.app_root()` now returns the install folder when the app is frozen and the repository root otherwise, and never uses the working directory. The `--validate` flag doubles as a smoke test: it loads the atlas from the frozen build and fails loudly if it can't.

### Making it smaller

The first working build was **628 MB**, which is absurd for a desktop pet. Most of it was one dependency:

| Step | Folder size |
| --- | ---: |
| First build (numpy with Intel MKL) | 628 MB |
| numpy with OpenBLAS instead | 116 MB |
| numpy removed | 73 MB |
| Unused standard-library modules excluded | **72 MB** |

numpy came with conda's MKL math libraries, which are about 400 MB. Swapping to OpenBLAS cut that, but the real question was why the app needed numpy at all. It was used in exactly one place, a scan that finds the opaque bounds of each frame. That is now a short pure-Python loop over row slices of the 82-frame atlas, so numpy is gone from the runtime environment. The test that checks content bounds still passes, so the result is the same. I am curious how much the test slows down without numpy, but it is only run on demand.

The build also excludes everything the app never imports (the art-pipeline tools, test packages, and parts of the standard library such as XML and compression). The installer itself, which compresses the folder, is **22.4 MB**.

Two things didn't shrink: OpenSSL (about 8 MB) is still bundled because the standard library's hashing module links to it, and the Qt libraries are most of what remains. Excluding both is possible, but I left them in for now because the saving didn't seem worth the risk of breaking something untested.

### The installer

The folder is wrapped with [Inno Setup](https://jrsoftware.org/isinfo.php) into `DeskPets-Setup-0.1.1.exe`. It installs per user, so it needs no administrator rights, adds a Start Menu shortcut, and has an uninstaller. "Start when I sign in to Windows" is offered as an option that is **off by default**, and it only touches the current user's startup entry. Settings live in `%APPDATA%\LC-pet-stat`, which the uninstaller leaves alone, so they survive both uninstalling and upgrading.

The last page of the installer has a "Launch DeskPets" box, **unticked by default**. I made it opt-in after a test on a clean virtual machine: the first start after installing is slow, because Windows Defender scans the new files, and the pet can take a noticeable while to appear. Starting it a second time was almost instant. That fits Defender scanning on first run, which I haven't isolated further. In my test, impatient double launches produced two pets, because the app doesn't stop a second copy from starting.

### What I tested on a clean machine

I ran the installer on a fresh Windows 11 virtual machine (Hyper-V), reverted to a clean checkpoint before each run. These all worked:

- **Install and run.** The app installs without administrator rights and runs.
- **Settings survive uninstalling.** They stay in `%APPDATA%\LC-pet-stat`, as designed.
- **Upgrading in place works.** Installing a newer build over the old one keeps the settings.
- **Quit leaves nothing behind.** After choosing Quit from the tray, no `DeskPets.exe` process remains.
- **Start when I sign in.** With the option ticked the app starts at sign-in, and with it unticked nothing is added. Uninstalling removes the entry.
- **Hover card and Pomodoro.** The stats card appears on hover, and the Pomodoro timer's ping plays when it finishes.
- **No NVIDIA GPU.** The virtual machine has no GPU at all, and the app runs normally without it.

### What isn't proven yet

- The installer is **unsigned**, so Windows SmartScreen will warn when it is downloaded.
- The first start after installing can be slow while Windows scans the files. This is expected to affect any freshly installed program, but I've only seen it in one virtual machine.
- The app is still in early development and needs to be tried on other people's machines, not just mine and one virtual machine.
